tickets.subject: Generation stalls at ~60% with Anthropic provider
tickets.body: Running QBORT 0.1.0 on macOS 15.3, generating 200 tickets against Claude via the Anthropic provider. Around batch 6 of 10 the progress bar freezes and never advances. Console shows "fetch failed: ETIMEDOUT" once, then nothing. The partial tickets.json does get written but stops at 118 tickets. Test connection passes fine before I start. Any way to make batches resume instead of hanging the whole run?

responses.body: Thanks for the detail, Priya. That ETIMEDOUT is the Anthropic call for one batch dropping and the orchestrator waiting on it. Can you tell me your batch size (Settings > Batching) and whether it reproduces at a smaller count like 40? I'd like to see if it's concurrency-related.
Batch size is 20, concurrency 4. At 40 tickets it finished clean twice in a row, no stall. It only wedges on the bigger runs.

That lines up with what we're seeing: a single timed-out batch currently blocks the pool instead of failing fast and retrying. Fix is landing in 0.1.1 to bound each batch with a timeout and re-queue it. As a workaround, drop concurrency to 2 for the 200-count run. I'll follow up here when the build is out.

tickets.subject: "QBORT is damaged and can't be opened" after download
tickets.body: Downloaded the 0.1.0 zip from the GitHub release and macOS 15.2 refuses to launch it — "QBORT is damaged and can't be opened. You should move it to the Trash." I understand the build is unsigned, but the usual right-click > Open trick isn't showing the Open option either. What's the supported way to get past Gatekeeper on this one?

tickets.subject: Exported tickets.json has malformed entries (trailing commas / cut off)
tickets.body: After a 150-ticket Ollama run using llama3.1:8b, the exported tickets.json won't parse — my loader throws "Unexpected token } in JSON" near the end. Opening it, the last ticket object looks truncated and there's a dangling comma. QBORT 0.1.0, macOS 14.6. Did the write get interrupted, or is the export not atomic?

responses.body: Sorry you hit that, Sofia. Writes are supposed to be atomic and coalesced, so a truncated file usually means the run errored mid-flight and the last partial batch got flushed. Was there anything in the app log around the end of the run — an Ollama disconnect or an out-of-memory from the model?
Now that I check the log, yes — "ollama: connection reset" right before it stopped. The Ollama server probably got OOM-killed on that machine.

That explains it. When the provider connection drops mid-batch we currently still write what assembled, which can leave a partial tail. The file should still be valid JSON though — a dangling comma is a real bug on our side, so I'm filing it. In the meantime, a smaller model or fewer concurrent batches will keep Ollama from getting killed.
Filed as a bug and linked to your ticket. Fix will ensure the on-disk file is always well-formed even when a run aborts partway. Thanks for the log line — that pinned it down fast.

tickets.subject: Add CSV export alongside tickets.json
tickets.body: We love using QBORT to seed our Zendesk sandbox, but the importer there wants CSV, not JSON. Right now I'm running a little jq script to convert every export, which is fine but flattening the nested responses is annoying. Could you add a native CSV export (one row per ticket, and ideally an option for one row per message)? Would save the whole team a step.

responses.body: Good request, Devon — CSV export is something we've heard before. Quick question so I can scope it right: for the message-per-row option, would you want the ticket-level fields (subject, status, customer) repeated on each message row, or a separate tickets file plus a messages file keyed by ticket id?
Repeated on each row would be ideal — single flat file is easiest for the Zendesk importer to map. Thanks for considering it.

tickets.subject: How is the staff-response distribution actually decided?
tickets.body: The docs mention a target number of staff responses per ticket, but I can't tell if that's an average across the run, a per-ticket exact count, or something weighted. I need my synthetic data to have a realistic spread of thread lengths for training a triage model. Where is this documented, and can I control the distribution?

responses.body: Great question, Hannah. The count you set is a per-ticket target the generator aims to match as closely as possible, applied ticket-by-ticket rather than as a run-wide average — so you'll see close-to-exact thread lengths, with small deviations when the model can't hit the number cleanly. To vary the spread today, adjust the target and re-run; a configurable distribution is on the roadmap. I've noted the doc is thin here and we'll expand it in the prompt-compiler section.
